title: Mock Exam 2
desc: The harder of the two mocks: situational judgment under pressure, with roughly a third of the questions set inside town government software problems where the tempting answer is the one a normal company would give.

questions.stem: Three stakeholders disagree about Ask the Ledger, the natural-language question box in your town budget product. Yusuf Adeyemi, the external auditor, calls it the single most valuable thing you have built. Dana Whitcomb, the Finance Director, would trade it tomorrow for saved views she trusts. Margaret Shaw, the Town Clerk, is frightened of it because a resident might be standing behind her when it runs. All three corner you and ask you to put the decision to a vote. What does Scrum say you should do?
options: Convene a standing product council of the three of them and adopt whatever the majority decides about Product Backlog order
Hand the decision to the Developers, since they are self-managing and best placed to judge what is feasible
Hear all three out, then decide the ordering yourself, because the Product Owner is one person and not a committee, and those wanting to change the Product Backlog do so by trying to convince you
Escalate to the Scrum Master, who is accountable for resolving conflicts between stakeholders
questions.explain: The Guide is unusually blunt here: 'The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.' The product council in option A is the most tempting distractor because it looks collaborative and democratic, and plenty of real companies run exactly that meeting. It is still wrong: it moves an accountability that belongs to one person into a group, which means nobody is accountable when the ordering turns out badly. Option B confuses self-management, which covers who does what, when, and how the work gets done, with deciding what is worth building. Option D invents a Scrum Master duty that does not exist; the Scrum Master facilitates stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed, but does not arbitrate product decisions.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Topic One of Sprint Planning, 'Why is this Sprint valuable?'
options: The Developers size the selected Product Backlog items so the Product Owner can judge the return on the Sprint
The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint, and the whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal
The Product Owner writes the Sprint Goal before the event and presents it to the Developers for acknowledgement
The Scrum Master derives the Sprint Goal from the Product Goal and confirms it with stakeholders
questions.explain: The Guide splits this precisely: the Product Owner proposes, the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal. Option C is the distractor that catches most people, because in practice a Product Owner usually walks in with a draft goal, and that is fine as a proposal. What is not fine is calling the draft the Sprint Goal. A goal handed down is not a goal the Developers can commit to, and the Sprint Goal is their commitment. Option A describes sizing, which is refinement work and belongs to the Developers, not Topic One. Option D moves a Scrum Team decision to the Scrum Master, who facilitates but does not author product objectives.

questions.stem: Each Scrum artifact contains a commitment. Which pairing is correct?
options: Product Backlog and Product Goal, Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal, Increment and Definition of Done
Product Backlog and Definition of Done, Sprint Backlog and Product Goal, Increment and Sprint Goal
Product Backlog and Sprint Goal, Sprint Backlog and Definition of Done, Increment and Product Goal
Product Backlog and Product Goal, Sprint Backlog and Definition of Done, Increment and Sprint Goal
questions.explain: Straight from the Scrum Artifacts section: 'For the Product Backlog it is the Product Goal. For the Sprint Backlog it is the Sprint Goal. For the Increment it is the Definition of Done.' Option D is the near miss that catches people who remember the Product Goal pairing and then guess, because Definition of Done feels like it belongs to a plan and Sprint Goal feels like it belongs to a result. It is the other way round: the Definition of Done is the quality bar the Increment must clear, and the Sprint Goal is the single objective the Sprint plan exists to serve. Commitments exist to add transparency and focus, so that progress against each artifact can be measured.

questions.stem: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing which of the following?
options: The number of Product Backlog items completed each Sprint
The value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
The utilization of the Developers across the Sprint
The accuracy of the release forecast given to stakeholders
questions.explain: Verbatim: 'The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.' Notice the exact scope. Not the value of everything the organization does, and not the value of the Developers' effort, but the value of the product that comes out of this team's work. Option A is the throughput trap: shipping more items is output, and output is not value. Option C is a resource-manager framing that Scrum does not contain anywhere; the Product Owner does not manage people. Option D is genuinely useful in the real world and still wrong here, because a forecast is a byproduct of empiricism, not the thing being maximized.

questions.stem: Scrum is founded on which of the following?
options: Empiricism and lean thinking
Empiricism and defined process control
Lean thinking and continuous delivery
Transparency, inspection, and adaptation
questions.explain: 'Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed. Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials.' Option D is the strongest distractor by a wide margin, because transparency, inspection, and adaptation are the most famous three words in Scrum. But they are the pillars, which are how empiricism gets implemented, not the foundation itself. The exam likes this distinction because it separates people who memorized a poster from people who read the text. Option B is a contradiction: defined process control is the opposite approach, the one that assumes you can specify everything up front.

questions.stem: A Product Owner at a civic software company has been assigning sizes to Product Backlog items himself, on the grounds that he understands the municipal domain better than anyone and can therefore judge effort faster. What does the Scrum Guide say about sizing?
options: The Product Owner sizes items so that ordering can reflect cost of delay
The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing, and the Product Owner may influence them by helping them understand and select trade-offs
The Scrum Master sizes items to keep the estimate neutral and free of stakeholder pressure
Sizing must be done in story points, which the Scrum Guide names as the sizing unit for Product Backlog items
questions.explain: The Guide says exactly: 'The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.' Option A is the tempting one, because domain expertise really does help and the Product Owner really does own ordering. But ordering and sizing are different jobs, and a size produced by someone who will not do the work is a guess dressed as data, which corrodes transparency. Option D fails on a single decisive word: the Guide never says story points, and in fact never uses the word estimate at all. It says 'size' and 'sizing'.

questions.stem: Who attends the Sprint Review?
options: Only the Scrum Team, so that the discussion can be candid
The Scrum Team and key stakeholders
Everyone in the organization, with attendance mandatory
The Product Owner and stakeholders, while the Developers keep working
questions.explain: 'The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.' The whole point is inspection by the people receiving the work, which is why option A fails: a Sprint Review with no stakeholders inspects nothing new. Option D is the antipattern that shows up constantly in real companies, where the Product Owner becomes a proxy and the people who built the thing never hear the reaction. The 2020 Guide deliberately dissolved that proxy pattern by making the Scrum Team a single unit. Option C overreaches: key stakeholders, not the entire organization, and nothing in Scrum makes attendance mandatory for people outside the Scrum Team.

questions.stem: True or false: the Sprint Review is the final event of the Sprint.
questions.explain: False. 'The Sprint Review is the second to last event of the Sprint.' The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. This is a memorization question and the exam asks it because the Sprint Review feels like an ending: stakeholders show up, results are shown, the room claps. But Scrum deliberately puts the Retrospective after it, so the team can inspect how it worked while the Review feedback is still fresh, and so the Sprint ends on adaptation rather than on applause.

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following are things the Scrum Guide states about the Product Owner accountability? Select three.
options: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
The Product Owner may delegate Product Backlog management work to others and remains accountable
The Product Owner is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness
The Product Owner is accountable for ordering Product Backlog items
The Product Owner is accountable for the Developers meeting the Definition of Done
questions.explain: Options A, B and D are all direct Guide statements. Option C is the trap, and it is a good one, because it sounds like something a senior product person should own. It is the Scrum Master's: 'The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness.' Option E fails on the same kind of boundary: 'The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done', and Developers are accountable for 'instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done'. The Product Owner does not police quality. Notice how B works: delegation moves the work, never the accountability. A Product Owner who has someone else write every item is still on the hook for those items being clear and understood.

questions.stem: In Ledgerline, your town budget product, the Budget Pace screen reports four departments trending over budget and the Executive Overview screen reports three. Both screens shipped, both passed review, and the printed packet for tonight's Northfield Select Board meeting was generated from one of them. What has most fundamentally gone wrong in Scrum terms?
options: A defect slipped through, which is a testing problem rather than a Scrum problem
The Definition of Done did not create the shared understanding of completeness it exists to create, so the Increment's transparency is compromised
The Product Owner failed to accept the items before they were released
The Sprint Goal was written too vaguely to hold the two screens together
questions.explain: 'The Definition of Done creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.' Two screens that disagree about the same fact means the shared understanding was never actually shared, and everyone inspecting the product now has a different basis for adaptation. Option A is the most tempting because it is what an engineering manager would say and it is true as far as it goes. Scrum still reads it as a transparency failure first, because artifacts with low transparency lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk, and a Select Board just made a decision on one of those numbers. Option C imports an acceptance step the Guide does not contain; the word reject appears zero times, and the Definition of Done has already made that call.
questions.cite: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

questions.stem: Margaret Shaw, the Northfield Town Clerk, currently spends around five hours servicing a single deep public-records request, and most of those requests turn out to be about vendor payments she could publish once and stop answering. Nothing in the product serves this today. Using Evidence-Based Management, which Key Value Area does that five-hour gap most directly describe?
options: Current Value, because it quantifies what the product delivers today
Unrealized Value, because it is the satisfaction gap between a beneficiary's desired outcome and their current experience
Time-to-Market, because it quantifies how quickly the organization can deliver and learn
Ability to Innovate, because it quantifies what prevents new capabilities from reaching users
questions.explain: Unrealized Value covers 'the potential future value that could be realized if the organization met the needs of all potential customers or users', and the EBM Guide defines it as the satisfaction gap between a beneficiary's desired outcome and their current experience. That is exactly a five-hour manual process the product does not touch yet. Option A is the strong distractor because the pain is happening right now, which makes it feel current. Current Value considers only what exists right now in the product, not the value that might exist. Time-to-Market and Ability to Innovate are organizational capability measures, about how fast and how effectively you can deliver, not about the size of the customer's unmet need.

questions.stem: A founder acting as Product Owner wants to join the Daily Scrum every day so he can answer questions on the spot and re-order the day's work when a sales call changes his mind. He is not working on any Sprint Backlog item. What is the best response?
options: This is good practice, because a highly available Product Owner unblocks the Developers faster

The Daily Scrum is a fifteen-minute event for the Developers, the Product Owner participates only as a Developer and only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items, and in no case does anyone from outside re-plan the Developers' day for them
The Product Owner must attend the Daily Scrum in order to report Product Backlog changes to the Developers
The Scrum Master should prevent all contact between the Product Owner and the Developers during the Sprint
questions.explain: 'The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.' The event exists so the Developers can inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and produce an actionable plan for the next day, and 'This creates focus and improves self-management.' Option A is the most tempting distractor because availability genuinely is a Product Owner virtue, and the Guide never says the Product Owner is banned from the room. What it says is whose event it is and in what capacity anyone else is present. The second half of the correct option is the part that actually matters: re-planning the Developers' day is not a Product Owner activity in any event. Option D swings to the opposite extreme and would destroy the collaboration the framework depends on.

questions.stem: During a live demo, the finance system feed shows an Error state, last synced two days ago, zero records today. It is visible only if you open a secondary tab that nobody opens. Every budget figure elsewhere in the product is silently derived from that feed. Which Scrum pillar failed first?
options: Inspection, because nobody was reviewing the feed status often enough
Adaptation, because nobody changed anything once the error appeared
Transparency, because the real state of the work and the product was not visible to those inspecting it
None of them, because a broken integration is an operational incident rather than a Scrum concern
questions.explain: The pillars run in order and the Guide is explicit about the dependency: 'Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.' People were inspecting budget numbers every day. Those numbers were confidently wrong. Every inspection built on them was therefore worse than useless, because it produced false confidence. Option A is the tempting one, and it is the answer most people give, because the surface symptom is that nobody noticed. But increasing the frequency of inspection on an invisible signal does not help. You have to make the state visible first. Option D is the practitioner's reflex and it is exactly the reflex the exam is testing: an artifact that misrepresents reality is a transparency problem regardless of the technical cause.

questions.stem: Returning to the query tool disagreement: the auditor wants it, the Finance Director is indifferent, and the Clerk objects only because residents can see her screen. As Product Owner, which approach is most consistent with your accountability?
options: Cut the feature, because two of the three stakeholders are not asking for it
Keep it exactly as built for everyone, because the auditor is the most technically sophisticated stakeholder and understands its value best

Notice that the disagreement is about exposure rather than existence, create separate Product Backlog items for the capability and for who can see it, order them, and decide, while representing the needs of all three in the Product Backlog
Put it to a vote at the next Sprint Review and let the attendees decide
questions.explain: 'The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog.' Representing needs is not the same as tallying preferences, and the skill being tested is hearing what the objection actually is. The Clerk is not objecting to the feature, she is objecting to who can see it, which is a different item. Option A is the tempting one because it looks responsive and decisive, and cutting scope always feels like discipline. It throws away value the auditor named as core in order to solve a visibility problem. Option D is the committee trap again in a new costume: the Sprint Review is a working session for inspecting the Increment and collaborating on what to do next, not a ballot.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide lists what effective Product Backlog management includes. Which THREE of the following appear on that list? Select three.
options: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items
Ordering Product Backlog items
Sizing Product Backlog items so the Developers can forecast
Approving Product Backlog items once the Developers complete them
questions.explain: The list has exactly four bullets: developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal, creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items, ordering Product Backlog items, and ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood. The first three are here. Option D is the sharpest distractor because sizing genuinely is Product Backlog work, it is just not the Product Owner's: 'The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing.' Option E imports an approval gate that does not exist anywhere in the 2020 Guide. Completion is settled by the Definition of Done, not by a signature.

questions.stem: An IT Director at a prospective municipal customer insists that your Product Owner must personally author every Product Backlog item, so the audit trail shows one accountable author. What is the most accurate response?
options: Agree, because the Product Owner is accountable for creating Product Backlog items and an accountability cannot be delegated
Explain that the Product Owner may delegate the authoring to others and remains accountable for the items being clear, ordered, and understood
Refuse, and explain that the Product Backlog belongs to the Developers because they do the work
Ask the Scrum Master to write the items, so that authorship and accountability sit with different people
questions.explain: 'The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.' Option A is the trap that catches careful readers, because it correctly quotes 'creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items' and then draws the wrong conclusion from it. Accountability and the work are separable in exactly one direction: you can hand off the work, you cannot hand off the accountability. Option C is false on its face; the Product Backlog is managed by the Product Owner, though anyone may contribute to it. Option D deliberately splits what Scrum deliberately joins.

questions.stem: Halfway through a Sprint whose Sprint Goal is 'Priya Raman, the Northfield Treasurer, can reconcile last month's warrant against the bank without leaving the product', the Developers discover the bank file format is different from what they assumed and roughly a third of the planned work is now wrong. What should happen?
options: The Product Owner cancels the Sprint, because the plan is no longer valid
The Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint, without affecting the Sprint Goal
The Product Owner rewrites the Sprint Goal to describe what is now achievable
The Sprint is extended so the original scope can still be delivered
questions.explain: 'If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.' The Sprint Goal is stable, the item list is not. Option C is the most tempting because it feels honest and adaptive, and it is what most teams actually do. It is wrong: the Sprint Goal is finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning and cannot change during the Sprint, which is precisely what makes it useful as a commitment. Option A is a real Product Owner power but the trigger has not fired; a Sprint may be cancelled when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and here the goal is still exactly as valuable as it was. Option D violates the fixed-length rule.

questions.stem: True or false: the Product Goal is contained in the Product Backlog.
questions.explain: True. 'The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define what will fulfill the Product Goal.' This one is worth burning in, because a lot of pre-2020 material has no Product Goal at all and a lot of tooling puts the goal in a slide deck or a vision document somewhere off to the side. In Scrum it lives inside the artifact, which is what makes the whole backlog readable as an argument about one objective rather than a pile of requests.

questions.stem: In Evidence-Based Management, which pair are described as the market value Key Value Areas, reflecting customer outcomes?
options: Current Value and Unrealized Value
Time-to-Market and Ability to Innovate
Current Value and Time-to-Market
Unrealized Value and Ability to Innovate
questions.explain: The EBM Guide splits the four areas into two pairs: 'Market value KVAs (UV, CV) reflect customer outcomes. Whereas, organizational capability KVAs (A2I, T2M) reflect the organization's ability to deliver valuable customer outcomes.' Current Value is what the product delivers today, Unrealized Value is what it could deliver if you met more of the need. Both are about the customer. Time-to-Market and Ability to Innovate are both about you: how fast you can learn, and what is stopping you from delivering new capability. Option C is the common miss, because Time-to-Market sounds customer facing when you say it out loud.
questions.cite: Evidence-Based Management Guide 2024, Key Value Areas

questions.stem: For a one-month Sprint, which THREE of the following timeboxes does the Scrum Guide state? Select three.
options: Sprint Planning, a maximum of eight hours
Sprint Review, a maximum of four hours
Sprint Retrospective, a maximum of three hours
Daily Scrum, a maximum of thirty minutes
Product Backlog refinement, a maximum of two hours
questions.explain: Eight, four, three, in descending order, for a one-month Sprint, and 'For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.' Option D is wrong on a single number: the Daily Scrum is a fifteen-minute event. Option E is the more interesting distractor, because refinement has no timebox at all. It is not an event. It is 'an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size', which is why the Guide never gives it a maximum duration. Anyone who has been to a weekly refinement meeting will feel like it is an event, and the exam knows that.

questions.stem: A founder who is also the Product Owner has deep domain knowledge of municipal finance. In Sprint Planning he begins specifying the architecture for the reconciliation engine, because he believes his domain knowledge makes his design better. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: This is appropriate, since the Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product and architecture determines value

For each selected Product Backlog item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment, and how this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers, because no one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value
The Scrum Master should specify the approach in order to shield the Developers from stakeholder pressure
Topic Three of Sprint Planning is jointly owned by the Product Owner and the Developers, so shared design is expected
questions.explain: The Guide uses one of its rare absolutes here: 'How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.' Option D is the strongest distractor because Sprint Planning as a whole is collaborative, the plan 'is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team', and Topics One and Two genuinely are shared. Topic Three is not. The Product Owner is still in the room and still answers questions, but the how belongs to the Developers. Option A is the classic founder trap: value accountability does not become design authority. Option C invents a Scrum Master technical role that does not exist.

questions.stem: For all twelve Northfield departments, the Budget Pace screen printed 'zero watch' no matter what the underlying data did, because the watch threshold could never be crossed given how it was calculated. The legend on screen showed watch as a live state the whole time. Which sentence from the Scrum Guide most precisely names the harm?
options: Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful
Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless
Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking
Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing
questions.explain: Every person who looked at that legend believed they were seeing a state that could occur. They were inspecting a fiction, so the inspection was misleading, and every minute spent on it was waste. That is the exact sentence. Option B is the near miss and it is a genuinely good sentence for a different failure: a team that inspects honestly and then changes nothing. Here the problem is upstream of that, in what was visible. Option D applies when a team sees a problem and cannot act, which is not what happened. The teachable pattern: when a question describes something that looked right but was not true, reach for transparency before anything else.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Sprint Backlog?
options: A list of tasks the Product Owner assigns to Developers at the start of the Sprint
The Sprint Goal, the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment, forming a plan by and for the Developers
A fixed contract for the Sprint, agreed at Sprint Planning and not changed until the Sprint ends
The top slice of the Product Backlog, maintained by the Scrum Master for reporting purposes
questions.explain: The Guide gives it as why, what and how: 'The Sprint Backlog is composed of the Sprint Goal (why), the set of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what), as well as an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how).' Option C is the most tempting because commitment language makes people think frozen. The Guide says the opposite: 'the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.' What is protected during a Sprint is the Sprint Goal, not the item list. Option A is project-manager framing, which the exam plants constantly. Option D gets the ownership wrong; it is a plan by and for the Developers.

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks that the product demo always display today's date. The demo data is seventy-five percent consumed against a July to June fiscal year, which pins the snapshot to a specific month. Switching to the live clock would make every projection, pace flag, and at-risk figure on the screen wrong. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Implement the request, because the stakeholder is the customer and the Product Owner serves the customer
Decline without further discussion, because ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's decision and is not open to negotiation
Make the trade-off and the arithmetic behind it visible, so the stakeholder can choose with the same information the Product Owner has, then decide
Pass the request to the Developers, since they built the calculation and understand the consequences
questions.explain: Transparency is not a reporting duty, it is the precondition for anyone making a good decision: 'The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work.' A stakeholder who does not know that the live clock breaks every projection is not making a bad decision, they are making an uninformed one, and closing that gap is your job before deciding. Option B is the tempting one for anyone who has just learned that the Product Owner decides. Deciding is yours; deciding in the dark, or leaving the other party in the dark, wastes the very thing that makes the decision defensible. Option A abdicates the accountability, and option D routes a product decision to the Developers.

questions.stem: True or false: Product Backlog refinement is a Scrum event with its own timebox.
questions.explain: False. Scrum has exactly five events: the Sprint, and inside it Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective. Refinement is 'an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size.' Teams very often hold a recurring refinement session, which is a perfectly reasonable practice, but the practice is not the framework. The exam uses this to separate people who learned Scrum from a calendar invite from people who read the Guide.

questions.stem: Two weeks into a four-week Sprint, the town that the entire Sprint Goal was built around withdraws from the pilot. The Sprint Goal is now genuinely obsolete. Who has the authority to cancel the Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master, who is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness
The Developers, since the Sprint Backlog is their plan and they can see it is now pointless
Only the Product Owner
The Scrum Team by consensus, since the whole team owns the Sprint
questions.explain: 'A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.' This matters because the usual exam heuristic, that sentences beginning with 'only the Product Owner' are traps, fails here. This is the one real absolute about the Product Owner in the whole Guide, and students who have been trained to distrust absolutes reliably get it wrong. Option D is the most tempting, because the 2020 Guide emphasizes one cohesive team and shared accountability everywhere else. Cancellation is the deliberate exception. Note also the trigger: the Sprint Goal being obsolete, not the Sprint going badly.

questions.stem: Your company's whole positioning is spending transparency. You discover that the large city you are targeting already built and publicly celebrated its own spending transparency portal, and that what it actually struggles with is enforcing prompt payment upstream in procurement. Which response is most consistent with a Product Owner maximizing value?
options: Sell harder on the existing positioning, since the product is already built and rebuilding is waste

Treat the current positioning as a hypothesis this market has refuted, and adapt the Product Backlog ordering and, if warranted, the Product Goal, because the adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation
Add features until the product beats the city's portal on the same dimension it already covers
Ask the Developers to choose which market to pursue, since they are self-managing and choose what to work on
questions.explain: 'If any aspects of a process deviate outside acceptable limits or if the resulting product is unacceptable, the process being applied or the materials being produced must be adjusted. The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation.' You have new evidence that the product as positioned is unacceptable to this market. Sitting on that is not patience, it is deviation. Option A is the sunk-cost distractor and it is very tempting because the code exists and reordering feels like waste. Option C is the trap of competing on the axis where the customer already has a solution, which is the most expensive way to be second. Option D misreads self-managing: the team decides who, how, and what work it takes on within the Sprint, not which market the company serves.

questions.stem: True or false: a Scrum Team may operate without a Scrum Master if the Developers are experienced and genuinely self-managing.
questions.explain: False. 'The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers.' There is no experience-based exemption. The End Note closes the door: 'While implementing only parts of Scrum is possible, the result is not Scrum.' In real life plenty of good teams run without a Scrum Master, and they may even do well, and that is exactly why the question is asked this way. The exam is not asking whether it can work. It is asking whether it is Scrum.

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following statements about the Increment are correct? Select three.
options: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint
An Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint
Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done
The Sprint Review is the gate at which an Increment becomes releasable
An Increment is complete once the Product Owner has signed it off
questions.explain: All three correct options are direct Guide sentences. Option D is contradicted about as directly as the Guide ever contradicts anything: 'The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.' That sentence exists because so many organizations turn the Review into a release approval meeting, which delays value for no empirical reason. Option E is the acceptance myth: the word reject appears zero times in the 2020 Guide, and the decision about completeness was already made by the Definition of Done. If it met the Definition of Done, an Increment was born at that moment, with no signature involved.

questions.stem: A Select Board meets twice a month, so the Scrum Team proposes running six-week Sprints so that every Sprint Review lands on a board meeting night. How should this be assessed?
options: Acceptable, since Sprint length should be set to match the cadence of the people receiving the work
Not Scrum, because Sprints are fixed length events of one month or less
Acceptable, provided the Product Owner approves the longer cadence
Acceptable, provided a separate stakeholder review is held every four weeks
questions.explain: 'They are fixed length events of one month or less to create consistency.' There is no approval that buys you a longer Sprint. The reasoning is given right there: 'When a Sprint's horizon is too long the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise, and risk may increase.' Option A is genuinely tempting, because aligning to stakeholder rhythm is real product thinking and would make the Reviews better attended. The fix is the other direction: keep the Sprint at a month or less, and invite the board to whichever Review they can reach, or bring the Increment to them, since an Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint anyway.

questions.stem: A Scrum Team has run every event on schedule for six months. The Retrospectives are well attended and produce a written list every time. Nothing about how the team works has changed in that period. What does the Scrum Guide say about this?
options: This is acceptable, provided a usable Increment is delivered each Sprint
Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless, and Scrum events are designed to provoke change
This is a Scrum Master failure, and the remedy is to replace the Scrum Master
This is acceptable if stakeholders report that they are satisfied
questions.explain: Two sentences, back to back: 'Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. Scrum events are designed to provoke change.' A Retrospective that reliably produces a list and never produces a change is theatre. Option A is the strongest distractor because delivering an Increment every Sprint is a real achievement and a lot of teams never manage it. It still does not excuse the missing half of empiricism; the purpose of the Retrospective is 'to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness', and a plan nobody enacts is not a plan. Option C jumps to a personnel remedy the Guide does not prescribe.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are given in the Evidence-Based Management Guide as example measures under Time-to-Market? Select two.
options: Release Frequency
Lead Time
Customer Satisfaction
Innovation Rate
Potential Market Share
questions.explain: Release Frequency and Lead Time are both Time-to-Market examples: how quickly you can deliver and learn from feedback. Customer Satisfaction is a Current Value measure, Innovation Rate is an Ability to Innovate measure, and Potential Market Share is an Unrealized Value measure. One caveat worth carrying into the real exam: the EBM Guide states plainly that 'To encourage adaptability, EBM defines no specific Key Value Measures.' These are illustrations of the kind of thing that belongs in each area, not a required set, so any question phrased as 'which measure must a team use' has no correct positive answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a way the Scrum Guide says the Scrum Master serves the organization?
options: Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams
Deciding which stakeholders the Product Owner is permitted to meet with
Owning the stakeholder communication plan on the Product Owner's behalf
Screening stakeholder requests before they are allowed into the Product Backlog
questions.explain: The organization-facing list is leading and training and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption, planning and advising Scrum implementations, helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work, and removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams. Notice the direction of travel: removing barriers, not building them. Options B, C and D are all gatekeeping, and all three are common real-world Scrum Master behaviours that the Guide points the other way on. The one that catches most people is D, because filtering noise feels protective. It puts a person between stakeholders and the Product Owner, and the Guide says anyone wanting to change the Product Backlog does so by trying to convince the Product Owner directly.

questions.stem: A grant lets a civic software company hire nine more people. The single Scrum Team would become sixteen people working on the same product. What does the Scrum Guide advise?
options: Form a discovery sub-team and a delivery sub-team within the Scrum Team so each can focus
Keep one team of sixteen, since the Guide asks for a team large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint
Consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product, sharing the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner
Reorganize into multiple Scrum Teams, each with its own Product Owner and Product Backlog, to reduce coordination overhead
questions.explain: 'If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.' Option D is the most tempting because it is what most organizations actually do, and it looks like it reduces coupling. It splits the product into pieces nobody owns as a whole and produces exactly the divergent, uncoordinated result Scrum is trying to avoid. Option A is worse in a quieter way: 'Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies.' Also worth noting the wording: typically ten or fewer, and consider reorganizing. Nothing here is a hard cap.

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following does the Scrum Guide state must hold during a Sprint? Select three.
options: No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal
Quality does not decrease
The Product Backlog is refined as needed
Scope is frozen once Sprint Planning has ended
The Sprint may be extended if the Sprint Goal is nearly achieved
questions.explain: The Guide gives four bullets for during the Sprint, three of which are here, and the fourth is the one that kills option D: 'Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.' That distinction is a favourite exam target. What is protected during a Sprint is the Sprint Goal, not the list of items, and people conflate the two constantly. Option E contradicts the fixed length rule. Read option B carefully too: quality does not decrease is an absolute, and it is why deadline-driven shortcuts through the Definition of Done are never sanctioned by the framework, no matter who approves them.

questions.stem: A government software organization publishes a Definition of Done that all its Scrum Teams must meet, including accessibility and security checks. Your team finds it heavy and wants to adopt a lighter one of its own. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: The team may use its own Definition of Done if the Product Owner agrees it maximizes value
If the Definition of Done is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum
Organizational Definitions of Done are advisory, since the Definition of Done is a Scrum Team commitment
The Scrum Master decides which Definition of Done applies to the team
questions.explain: Verbatim: 'If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.' The decisive words are 'as a minimum'. A team may add to it and may never subtract from it. Option A is the most tempting because Product Owner plus value sounds like it should win, and because the Definition of Done really is a Scrum Team commitment when no organizational standard exists. It is not a Product Owner decision in either case; the Developers are the ones required to conform to it.
questions.cite: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

questions.stem: Your Anomaly Review screen flags unusual town transactions, but Dana Whitcomb, the Finance Director, cannot see the rule behind a flag or clear a false positive, and Angela Pike, the clerk who works the screen daily, can only look at it. You have one engineer. The choice is between building three new detection rules and finishing the workflow around the flags that already exist. Which reasoning best fits your accountability?
options: Build the new detection rules, because more detection means more value surfaced
Order the work by what most increases the value of the product, which here means making existing flags actionable, and make that reasoning visible in the ordering of the Product Backlog
Let the Developers choose, since they are self-managing and will pick whichever is more tractable
Split the Sprint so that half the capacity goes to each, so neither stakeholder group is disappointed
questions.explain: Two Guide lines carry this. You are accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and for 'ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood'. A flag nobody can act on delivers no value, so more flags multiply an existing zero. Option A is the tempting one because detection is the visible, demonstrable feature and finishing a workflow is unglamorous. Option D is the worse trap and the one founders reach for under pressure: splitting capacity to avoid a hard conversation produces two half-finished things, which is the ordering decision you were accountable for making, made badly and invisibly.

questions.stem: Your team reports fourteen Product Backlog items Done last Sprint. No municipality is yet using the product for anything real. A stakeholder asks whether the Sprint was successful. Which reading is most consistent with the Scrum Guide?
options: It was successful, because throughput was high and the process is therefore healthy

Items Done are output; the entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint, and an Increment provides value only if it is usable and is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal
It was unsuccessful, which means the Definition of Done is too weak
It was unsuccessful, which means the Sprint length needs to change
questions.explain: 'The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint', and 'An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal... In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable.' Fourteen items is a count of output. The question Scrum asks is whether the product moved toward its goal in a way someone can use. Option A is the metric trap and it is extremely tempting because throughput is measurable and comforting. Options C and D are both plausible diagnoses in the real world but neither follows from the facts given; they leap to a remedy without the evidence, which is the opposite of empiricism.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: To inspect the Increment with stakeholders and gather feedback on the product
To plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness
To review whether the Sprint forecast was met and account for the variance
To re-order the Product Backlog in light of what was learned during the Sprint
questions.explain: One sentence, and the exam quotes it almost word for word: 'The purpose of the Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness.' Note both nouns. Quality is in there deliberately, which is why the Definition of Done is one of the things the team inspects. Option A describes the Sprint Review, and that swap is the single most common Retrospective mistake. Option C is the accountability-theatre version that many organizations actually run, and it is nowhere in the Guide. Option D happens continuously through refinement and at the Sprint Review; it is not the Retrospective's purpose.

questions.stem: Who is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The entire Scrum Team
The Developers together with the Scrum Master
questions.explain: 'The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.' Option A is the trap and it is a very good one, because the Developers really are 'committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint', and because pre-2020 material framed the Development Team as the delivery unit. The 2020 Guide dissolved the team-within-a-team on purpose, precisely so that value and delivery stop being separate people's problems. Read the words in the option carefully: valuable and useful, not just usable. Value cannot be the Developers' alone, and delivery cannot be the Product Owner's alone.

questions.stem: Two days before a council presentation, your team finds a calculation error that has been quietly wrong in every packet printed this quarter. Fixing it will make the current numbers look worse and will require telling the customer. Which Scrum Values most directly name what the situation demands?
options: Focus, so the team stays on the Sprint Goal rather than chasing a defect
Courage, to do the right thing and work on tough problems, together with Openness about the work and the challenges
Commitment, because the team promised the packet and must deliver it
Respect, because the team must trust the customer to handle the news later
questions.explain: The Guide describes Courage as having 'the courage to do the right thing, to work on tough problems' and Openness as the Scrum Team and its stakeholders being 'open about the work and the challenges'. Disclosing an error that makes you look bad, before someone else finds it, is precisely both. Option C is the most tempting distractor, because Commitment is a listed value and 'we promised' sounds like integrity. The Guide's Commitment is to goals and to supporting each other, not to shipping a known falsehood on schedule. Option D misuses Respect as a reason for delay, which is how values get quietly inverted in practice.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following statements about the Definition of Done are correct? Select two.
options: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born
If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review
The Product Owner defines the Definition of Done and may adjust it to reflect changing value
The Definition of Done may be relaxed for a Sprint when a stakeholder deadline requires it
The Definition of Done is another name for the acceptance criteria of an individual Product Backlog item
questions.explain: Both correct options are verbatim Guide sentences, and the second is stronger than most people remember: not only can undone work not be released, it cannot even be shown at the Sprint Review, and it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration. Option C is the tempting one, because the Product Owner owns value and quality feels like part of value. The Definition of Done is a Scrum Team commitment, and the Developers are required to conform to it. Option D collides with 'Quality does not decrease' during the Sprint. Option E confuses two different things: acceptance criteria are per item, the Definition of Done is the standard for the whole Increment.
questions.cite: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

questions.stem: Your discovery report treats Finance Director and Treasurer as two distinct personas with different needs and permissions. In a town the size of Northfield one human usually holds both jobs, and state law explicitly allows it. The Product Backlog is written against the two-persona model. What does this most directly threaten?
options: The Sprint Goal, which cannot be met by a product built on a wrong model
The transparency of the Product Backlog, because items written against a model that does not match real users lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk
The Definition of Done, which should have caught the mismatch
The Scrum Master's effectiveness, since coaching should have surfaced this
questions.explain: 'With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.' A backlog full of items that describe users who do not exist in that combination looks perfectly transparent and is quietly misleading, which is the worst kind. Option A is tempting because the consequence really does show up as missed goals, but that is downstream. Option C misplaces the Definition of Done, which is a quality standard for the Increment, not a check on whether your user model is true. This is also a useful reminder that personas are a practice, not part of Scrum, so nothing in the Guide obliges you to keep a clean persona model if a messy one is truer.

questions.stem: At the Sprint Review, the Finance Director asks to click through the new reconciliation screen herself. The team has prepared a slide walkthrough instead, because the screen is fiddly to drive live. What is the best correction?
options: Slides are appropriate, because the Sprint Review is where the Scrum Team presents its results
The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation, since attendees are meant to collaborate on what to do next
The Product Owner should present alone, so the Developers can continue working on the next Sprint
The Review should be postponed until the screen is polished enough to demonstrate reliably
questions.explain: 'The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.' The purpose is to inspect the outcome and determine future adaptations, and you cannot inspect a slide. Option A is the strongest distractor because the Guide really does say the Scrum Team presents the results of their work, and people stop reading at that clause. Presenting is the beginning of the event, not the shape of it. Option D is worse than it looks: postponing removes the inspection point entirely, and Scrum events are the cadence that makes inspection possible. Note also that the Increment shown must already meet the Definition of Done, so 'fiddly to drive' is itself a signal worth raising.

questions.stem: An organization has cut its deployment frequency and cycle time dramatically over two quarters. In the same period, customer satisfaction has fallen and no new market opportunity has been pursued. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say about this pattern?
options: Nothing is wrong, because capability improvements reliably precede value improvements

Targeting improvements only in Ability to Innovate and Time-to-Market without monitoring Current Value and Unrealized Value focuses on internal processes that may not further satisfy customers, and can indicate a lack of outcome-based goals
The organization should stop measuring Time-to-Market, since it is distracting from value
The Product Owner has failed and the Product Goal must be replaced
questions.explain: This is the EBM Guide's own balance warning, nearly word for word. The four Key Value Areas are meant to be read together: two about the customer, two about your capability to serve them. Getting faster at shipping things nobody wanted is a very efficient way to go nowhere. Option A is the tempting one because it is a genuinely common and often true belief, and it is exactly the belief the warning targets. Option C overcorrects: the answer is not to stop measuring capability, it is to stop measuring only capability. It is also worth remembering that measuring outputs and activities is easy while measuring outcomes is hard, which is why teams drift toward the easy half.
questions.cite: Evidence-Based Management Guide 2024, Key Value Areas

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide states that the Developers are always accountable for certain things. Which THREE of the following are on that list? Select three.
options: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog
Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done
Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal
Ordering the Product Backlog by value once it is sized
Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
questions.explain: The list has four bullets, three of which appear here; the fourth is 'Holding each other accountable as professionals'. Options D and E are both Product Owner accountabilities, and they are placed here because sizing and ordering feel adjacent to each other. They are not: Developers size, the Product Owner orders. Read option C closely, because it names the single most misunderstood thing about the Daily Scrum. The Developers adapt their plan every day toward the Sprint Goal. Nobody else adapts it for them, and the plan being adapted is theirs.

questions.stem: True or false: a new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
questions.explain: True, and stated exactly that way. There is no gap, no planning week, no stabilization period between Sprints. This is one of the structural reasons that Sprint Zero and hardening Sprints are not Scrum: there is nowhere for them to live, and every Sprint must produce a usable Increment anyway. The practical consequence for a Product Owner is that Sprint Planning has to be ready when the previous Sprint ends, which is a large part of why refinement is described as an ongoing activity rather than something you do the day before.

questions.stem: Every Ledgerline roadmap item from R-01 to R-16 is now clickable in a demo, each shipped as its own change. The one thing not built is the reconciliation tie-out that Priya Raman, the Treasurer, says determines whether she can use the product at all, because it needs a real backend. Which Scrum Guide statement most directly challenges calling the current build an Increment?
options: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal, and in order to provide value the Increment must be usable
The Sprint Review is the second to last event of the Sprint
The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product
Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint
questions.explain: Usable is the decisive word, and it is doing real work in that sentence. A demo that shows every feature and lets no one do their job is output, not an Increment, no matter how many items are Done. This is the trap the exam sets whenever a scenario emphasises how much was built. Option C is tempting because the situation clearly also involves ordering, and reordering is part of the remedy, but the question asks what challenges the claim that this is an Increment, and emergence does not speak to that. Option D is a real issue lurking in the background, since 'needs a real backend' hints at a missing skill, but it is a cause, not the challenge to the claim.

questions.stem: State law says a treasurer may disburse funds only on a warrant affirmatively voted and signed by a majority of the select board, and the Northfield Select Board meets twice a month. Your faster-payment feature must live inside that workflow, not around it. Where does that constraint belong?
options: In a separate compliance document outside the Product Backlog, since Scrum artifacts describe product work only

In the Product Backlog item itself, refined until the item is clear enough for the Developers to build something both legal and usable, because the Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team
In the Definition of Done, since every legal requirement is a quality measure that applies to the Increment
In the Sprint Goal, so that the team cannot forget it during the Sprint
questions.explain: 'The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.' Single source is the phrase that settles it: if the constraint shapes what gets built, it has to be visible where the work is decided. Refinement then does the rest, adding 'details, such as a description, order, and size'. Option C is the strongest distractor, and it is half right in spirit. The Definition of Done holds standards that apply to every Increment, like accessibility or security checks. A statutory workflow rule that applies to one feature is item-level content, not a universal quality bar, and burying it in the Definition of Done hides it from ordering decisions. Option A splits transparency across two places, which reliably means one of them goes stale.

questions.stem: A stakeholder insists that the Scrum Team must maintain a burndown chart because it is 'part of Scrum'. Which statement is correct?
options: Burndown charts are required in Scrum in order to track progress within the Sprint
Various practices exist to forecast progress, like burn-downs, burn-ups, or cumulative flows, and while proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism
Burndown charts are forbidden, because practices not named in the Scrum Guide are outside the framework
The Product Owner is accountable for maintaining the forecast chart for stakeholders
questions.explain: That is the Guide's sentence, and it is deliberately even handed: these practices are useful and none of them is mandatory. The next line is the one worth memorizing: 'In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.' Option C is the interesting distractor, because a lot of people over-correct once they learn that story points and velocity are not in the Guide, and start treating absence as prohibition. Scrum is purposefully incomplete and 'wraps around existing practices'. The rule is that a practice may not replace the framework, not that it is banned.

questions.stem: Tom Iverson, the Northfield Town Manager, tells you that the Select Board has reviewed your Product Backlog and directed the team to build the resident-facing portal ahead of the reconciliation work you had ordered first. What does the Scrum Guide say about this situation?
options: The Product Owner must comply, since the customer's governing body outranks the supplier's Scrum Team
The Developers should decide, since they are self-managing and choose what they work on
For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions; the Board may try to convince the Product Owner, and the decision remains the Product Owner's
The Scrum Master should cancel the Sprint and facilitate a reset of the Product Backlog order
questions.explain: 'For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.' The Board can bring evidence, argument, money, and urgency, and all of that is legitimate input. What it cannot do is reach into the ordering. Option A is the most tempting because in real commercial life the customer often does get their way, and because refusing a customer feels reckless. The Scrum answer is not that you ignore them, it is that you own the decision and stay answerable for it. Option D misuses cancellation, which requires the Sprint Goal to be obsolete.

questions.stem: After a hard Sprint, the team proposes a one-week Sprint with no new functionality, dedicated to cleaning up the anomaly rules and paying down shortcuts. How should this be assessed?
options: Acceptable, because Scrum permits special Sprint types when quality work is required
Not Scrum: every Sprint has the same shape and must produce a usable Increment, and cleanup work belongs in the Product Backlog to be ordered like everything else
Acceptable, because the Sprint Retrospective may add improvement items to the Sprint Backlog, which makes a dedicated improvement Sprint the same idea at a larger scale
Acceptable, provided the Scrum Master classifies it as impediment removal
questions.explain: There are no Sprint types in Scrum. Every Sprint is a container that produces a usable Increment, quality does not decrease during a Sprint, and work that does not meet the Definition of Done was never part of an Increment in the first place. A hardening Sprint is an admission that previous Sprints shipped undone work. Option C is the cleverest distractor here, because it is true that 'The most impactful improvements are addressed as soon as possible. They may even be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.' That sentence permits improvement items inside a normal Sprint. It does not authorize a Sprint made entirely of them with no Increment at the end.

questions.stem: A government procurement questionnaire asks whether you will hold a specific security certification by a named date. Internally, the controls are implemented but no audit has been conducted and every date on the compliance roadmap is a placeholder. Which response best fits the Product Owner accountability and Scrum's empiricism?
options: Commit to the date, because losing this contract destroys more value than an optimistic commitment risks
Say nothing about the future at all, because Scrum forbids forecasting in complex environments

Give an explicit forecast grounded in what has actually been completed, state plainly what has not been done, and let the buyer decide, because only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making
Take the date to Sprint Planning and have the Developers commit to it as the Sprint Goal
questions.explain: The Guide's sentence about forecasting is the whole answer: 'In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.' A forecast built on completed work is honest and useful. A date built on hope is a transparency failure that will be discovered by the customer rather than by you. Option A is the tempting one, and it is tempting precisely because the stakes are real. Notice what it actually proposes: buying a contract with a claim you have no evidence for. Option B is the caricature of empiricism; Scrum forecasts constantly, it just refuses to call a forecast a promise. Option D outsources a commercial commitment to the Developers, who cannot make it.

questions.stem: Mid-Sprint, an influential stakeholder emails two Developers directly asking them to squeeze in a small change 'since it is only a few hours'. What is the best handling?
options: The Developers implement it, since they are self-managing and closest to the code
The Scrum Master blocks stakeholder contact with the Developers for the rest of the Sprint
The request goes to the Product Owner, who decides whether and where it enters the Product Backlog, because those wanting to change the Product Backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner
The change waits until the Sprint Review, where attendees vote on whether it is worth doing
questions.explain: The Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team, and changes to it go through the Product Owner. Option A is the sharpest distractor because self-management is real and the change genuinely is small. Self-management covers how the Developers organize their work toward the Sprint Goal, not whether new product work enters the Sprint. Absorbing side requests is also how Sprint Goals quietly die. Option B overcorrects into gatekeeping, and the Scrum Master's listed duty runs the other way: 'Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.' Option D turns the Review into a ballot, which it is not.

questions.stem: True or false: an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.
questions.explain: True, and the Guide goes further in the same paragraph: 'The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.' Both sentences exist because organizations habitually turn the Review into a release approval meeting, which delays value with no empirical benefit. If the work meets the Definition of Done and the Product Owner judges it valuable to release, it can go out on a Tuesday. Also worth pairing with this: 'Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint', and the sum of them is what is presented at the Review.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are true of the Daily Scrum? Select two.
options: Its purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary
It is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint
The Developers must answer three specific questions about yesterday, today, and impediments
The Scrum Master must facilitate it every day so that it stays within its timebox
It is the only time the Developers are permitted to adjust their plan
questions.explain: The first two are Guide statements, and the reason given for the second is worth knowing: 'To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint.' Option C is a 2017 fossil. The revisions page lists 'removed Daily Scrum questions' explicitly, and the 2020 text says the Developers 'can select whatever structure and techniques they want'. A great deal of free practice material still teaches the three questions as required, which is exactly why it is here. Option E is contradicted directly: 'The Daily Scrum is not the only time Developers are allowed to adjust their plan.' Option D confuses ensuring events happen with personally running them.

questions.stem: Your own discovery research in Northfield concludes that operator trust comes from reconciliation and clear definitions, not from the tamper-evident record-keeping technology your company leads with in every pitch. What is the most defensible Product Owner response?
options: Set the finding aside, because company positioning is a strategy decision that sits outside the product
Quietly change the Product Goal to match the finding, without raising it with stakeholders, since ordering is your decision

Make the finding transparent to the Scrum Team and stakeholders, and adapt the Product Backlog ordering and, if warranted, the Product Goal, because a Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection
Add explanatory content to the product so users come to appreciate the differentiator
questions.explain: 'A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.' The hard part of this question is not the Scrum rule, it is that the evidence attacks your own story, which is exactly when people reach for option A or option D. Option D is the most seductive because it looks like action and preserves the narrative; it treats a validated finding about what customers value as a communication problem. Option B fails on a different axis and is the trap for people who have just internalized that the Product Owner decides: you do decide, and you also owe transparency, because artifacts exist so that everyone inspecting them has the same basis for adaptation.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide lists ways the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner. Which THREE of the following are on that list? Select three.
options: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items
Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed
Ordering the Product Backlog when the Product Owner is unavailable
Confirming the Sprint Goal before Sprint Planning concludes
questions.explain: The fourth item on the Guide's list is 'Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment'. Every one of them is help, technique, or facilitation. None of them is doing the Product Owner's job. Option D is the trap, and it is the one real teams fall into constantly when a Product Owner is stretched thin across sales and strategy. Ordering is a Product Owner accountability, and a Scrum Master who takes it over has not helped, they have made the accountability ambiguous. Option E invents an approval step; the Sprint Goal is defined collaboratively by the whole Scrum Team and finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning, with nobody confirming it from outside.

questions.stem: At a Daily Scrum the Developers realize that a core assumption behind the current approach is wrong. They decide to raise it at the Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint, so stakeholders and the Product Owner hear it at the same time. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: This is correct, because the Sprint Review is the formal inspection point where adaptations are determined
The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation, and a Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection
This is correct, because no changes may be made during a Sprint
The Scrum Master should decide when the information is disclosed, to protect the team's focus
questions.explain: Both quoted phrases come from the Adaptation section, and together they rule out saving up bad news for a scheduled event. Option A is genuinely tempting because the Sprint Review really is a formal inspect-and-adapt point, and holding information for it can feel orderly and respectful of everyone's attention. The cost is days of work built on a known-wrong assumption, which is the deviation the Guide tells you to minimize. Option C misstates the rule: what may not change is anything that would endanger the Sprint Goal, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned. That renegotiation is precisely the conversation these Developers should be having today.

questions.stem: An external auditor and two residents ask to sit in on Sprint Planning. What does the Scrum Guide allow?
options: Only the Scrum Team may attend Sprint Planning
The Scrum Team may invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice
Sprint Planning is open to all stakeholders by default, since transparency is a pillar
The Product Owner alone decides who attends, since the Product Owner owns what enters the Sprint
questions.explain: 'The Scrum Team may also invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice.' Two decisive words: may, and advice. It is optional, it is by invitation from the Scrum Team, and the guests advise rather than decide. Option A is the most commonly held wrong belief, because Sprint Planning feels like an internal event and people generalize from the Daily Scrum, which really is for the Developers. Option C confuses transparency with open attendance; transparency is about the state of the artifacts being visible, not about meeting access. Option D gives the invitation decision to one person when the Guide gives it to the Scrum Team.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are widely practiced but are NOT defined anywhere in the Scrum Guide 2020? Select two.
options: A Definition of Ready that Product Backlog items must satisfy before they can be selected in Sprint Planning
The Product Owner formally accepting or rejecting completed items at the Sprint Review
Product Backlog refinement as an ongoing activity
The Sprint Retrospective concluding the Sprint
The Sprint Goal being finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning
questions.explain: Options C, D and E are all Guide content. Option A is the one that trips careful readers, because the Guide does use the word ready once: 'Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event.' That describes a characteristic items acquire through refinement, not a formal gate with a checklist and a gatekeeper. Option B is the acceptance myth. The word reject appears zero times in the 2020 Guide, and the Definition of Done has already answered the question: an item that does not meet it cannot even be presented at the Sprint Review. Neither practice is forbidden, and neither is Scrum.
questions.cite: Scrum Guide 2020, Product Backlog and Commitment: Definition of Done

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Sprint Goal?
options: It is a commitment by the Product Owner that describes the scope agreed for the Sprint
It is the single objective for the Sprint, a commitment by the Developers, and it provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it
It is the list of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, expressed as one sentence
It is set by the Scrum Master to keep the Scrum Team focused on one thing at a time
questions.explain: All three clauses matter. Single objective, so a Sprint has one, not a themed collection. A commitment by the Developers, even though the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define it. And flexible about the exact work, which is what lets scope be renegotiated inside the Sprint without breaking the commitment. Option C is the most common real-world error, where a team writes a Sprint Goal that is just the ticket list strung into one line, which gives up every benefit: it cannot survive scope change, it does not tell stakeholders why the Sprint mattered, and it does not create the coherence and focus the Guide describes. Option A gets both the owner and the substance wrong.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are accurate statements about the Product Backlog? Select two.
options: It is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product
It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team
It is prioritized by the stakeholders and then approved by the Product Owner
It may contain only items small enough to be completed within a single Sprint
It is finalized at the start of each release and then held stable to protect the plan
questions.explain: Both correct options are verbatim. Option C fails on two decisive words at once: the Guide says ordered, not prioritized, a change made back in 2011, and the ordering is the Product Owner's accountability, not something stakeholders do and the Product Owner rubber-stamps. Option D confuses the whole backlog with its top: items that can be Done within one Sprint are 'deemed ready for selection', which is a property of the ones near the top after refinement, not a rule for the entire list. Option E contradicts emergent, and emergent is the word doing the most work in the definition: the backlog is never finished, because the product is never finished.

questions.stem: A company sets up a standing product council of the chief executive, the head of sales, and the Product Owner, which meets fortnightly and votes on Product Backlog order. Which statement best identifies the Scrum problem?
options: There is no problem, provided the Product Owner holds a veto
The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, so ordering decisions must remain with the Product Owner even though the needs of many stakeholders are represented in the Product Backlog
Committees are acceptable in Scrum provided the Scrum Master facilitates them
The problem is the chief executive's presence specifically, since seniority distorts the discussion
