questions.explain: 'The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.' Option A is the most tempting because a veto sounds like it preserves the accountability, and plenty of organizations describe their setup exactly that way. It does not survive contact with reality: a Product Owner who must spend political capital to overturn a vote is not making the decision, they are appealing it. The Guide names the healthy version of the same conversation, which is stakeholders trying to convince the Product Owner. That is a meeting worth having. What breaks it is the vote. Option D misdiagnoses the structure as a personality problem.

questions.stem: Which of the following may result from a Sprint Review?
options: The Product Owner formally signs off each completed Product Backlog item
The Product Backlog is adjusted to meet new opportunities, and attendees collaborate on what to do next
The Increment is released, since the Sprint Review is the release gate
The Sprint Backlog for the following Sprint is created, since planning follows review
questions.explain: 'The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities' and 'attendees collaborate on what to do next' are both in the Sprint Review section. That is what makes it a working session rather than a report. Option C is directly denied: 'The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.' Option D belongs to Sprint Planning, which happens in the next Sprint, and the Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. Option A is the acceptance myth once more; it is worth noticing how many plausible-sounding wrong answers in this exam are variations on the idea that someone signs off the work.

questions.stem: According to the Scrum Guide, what is a product?
options: A software application delivered to a paying customer
A vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders, and well-defined users or customers
Whatever a Scrum Team happens to be working on during the current Sprint
A bundle of features released together into a market
questions.explain: The Guide's definition sits inside the Product Goal section: 'A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined users or customers. A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.' The definition matters practically, because it is the test you apply when someone proposes that a component, a team, or an internal platform is 'the product'. If you cannot name its boundary, its stakeholders, and its users, you cannot write a Product Goal for it and you cannot order a backlog against it. Option A is the tempting narrow reading, and the Guide explicitly widens it beyond software.

questions.stem: A Scrum Team stops inviting stakeholders to the Sprint Review because their feedback is scattered and slows the session down. The Product Owner now collects feedback separately and relays it to the team. What is lost?
options: Nothing meaningful, provided the Product Owner is a faithful relay
The formal inspection of the Increment by the people receiving the work, which is what transparency exists to enable; adaptation now runs through one person's filter
The Sprint Goal, which cannot be evaluated without stakeholders present
The Definition of Done, which stakeholders are meant to agree at the Review
questions.explain: 'The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving the work', and the Sprint Review exists so the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect together and decide what to do next. Option A is the tempting one because a good Product Owner really can relay feedback well, and the 2017-era proxy model made exactly this arrangement look normal. The 2020 Guide dissolved that proxy pattern deliberately: it produces a team that never hears an unfiltered reaction and stakeholders who never see the real thing. Option D is a category error, since the Definition of Done is not a stakeholder agreement.

questions.stem: The Scrum Master is accountable for which of the following?
options: Managing the Scrum Team's work and personally removing every impediment the team encounters
Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness
Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood
Ensuring that the Sprint Goal is achieved by the end of the Sprint
questions.explain: Two accountabilities, stated in two consecutive paragraphs. Option A contains a real duty phrased wrongly: the Guide says 'Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress', and causing removal is very different from doing the removing. A Scrum Master who personally clears every obstacle produces a team that cannot function without them, which is the opposite of coaching self-management. Option C is a Product Owner accountability, one of the four Product Backlog management bullets. Option D belongs to nobody: the Sprint Goal is a commitment by the Developers, and Scrum has no guarantor of outcomes, which is rather the point of an empirical framework.

questions.stem: A Sprint ends with the reconciliation tie-out unfinished and not meeting the Definition of Done. What happens to it?
options: It carries over automatically into the next Sprint's Sprint Backlog, since the work is already underway
It returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration, where the Product Owner orders it against everything else
It is presented at the Sprint Review as partially complete so stakeholders can judge whether it is worth continuing
The Sprint is extended until the item is finished, so the effort is not wasted
questions.explain: 'If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.' Option A is the strongest distractor because carry-over is what almost every tool does by default and what almost every team says out loud. Scrum has no concept of spill-over, and the reason is an ordering reason rather than a bookkeeping one: the world changed during the Sprint, and unfinished work must re-earn its place against everything else, which is your decision. Option C is explicitly excluded by that same sentence. Option D breaks the fixed-length Sprint.
questions.cite: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide describes the framework as purposefully incomplete. What follows for a Product Owner who wants to use practices such as personas, story mapping, or split tests?
options: They are not permitted, because the Scrum framework is immutable
They may be used within the framework, which wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary, but they are not Scrum and cannot replace any part of it
They may replace Product Backlog refinement, since they produce more detailed information about items
They must be approved by the Scrum Master, who is accountable for establishing Scrum
questions.explain: Two sentences do the work: 'The Scrum framework is purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory' and 'Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary.' Option A is the over-correction that catches people who have just learned the End Note phrase about immutability. Immutable means you may not remove or alter the parts of Scrum, not that you may not add anything around it. Option C is the genuinely dangerous version, because a good practice quietly substituting for a framework element is how teams end up doing something that is not Scrum while believing they are. Option D invents an approval role.

questions.stem: True or false: if the Product Owner is actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate in the Daily Scrum as a Developer.
questions.explain: True, and stated almost exactly this way: 'If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.' Two things follow that the exam likes to test. First, the capacity matters, not the job title: the Product Owner is there as a Developer, inspecting progress toward the Sprint Goal, not as a stakeholder receiving a status report. Second, the condition is real. A Product Owner who is not working on Sprint Backlog items has no standing to participate in the Daily Scrum on that basis, because it is an event for the Developers.

questions.stem: Your Scrum Team is roughly halfway to a Product Goal about pilot towns closing their books without spreadsheets, when a much larger opportunity opens in a different state with different needs. Leadership wants both pursued. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: Pursue both Product Goals in parallel, since one Product Backlog can hold work for both

The Scrum Team must fulfill or abandon one objective before taking on the next, so if the new opportunity is the better objective, the current Product Goal is abandoned deliberately and visibly rather than quietly carried alongside
The Scrum Master decides which goal takes precedence, since they are accountable for the team's effectiveness
Create a second Scrum Team with its own Product Owner and Product Backlog for the new opportunity on the same product
questions.explain: 'The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.' Note the parenthesis: abandoning is explicitly allowed, and this question is really about doing it honestly. Option A is the most tempting because a backlog obviously can hold both, and because leadership asked for both. What it produces is a team that is 'focused on one objective at a time' in name only, which is the exact phrase the Guide uses about the Scrum Team. Option D breaks the multi-team rule, which requires teams on the same product to share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following statements about Sprint Planning are correct? Select two.
options: The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning
Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select the items from the Product Backlog to include in the Sprint
The Product Owner selects the items for the Sprint and the Developers decide how to build them
Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint
The Scrum Master is accountable for producing the resulting Sprint Backlog
questions.explain: Both correct options hinge on a single decisive word. In the first it is finalized, and prior to the end, so the Sprint may not begin with a goal still being drafted. In the second it is select: the Developers select, through discussion with the Product Owner, which is why option C is wrong even though it sounds like a reasonable division of labour and describes what many teams actually do. The Product Owner proposes value and orders the backlog; the people who will do the work decide how much of it they take on. Option D is the Sprint Review's timebox, not Sprint Planning's, which is eight hours. Option E misassigns an artifact the Developers own.

questions.stem: To hit a demo date for a prospective municipal customer, the team proposes dropping the accessibility and security checks from its Definition of Done for two Sprints and adding them back afterwards. The Product Owner supports it because the deal is large. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: This is acceptable, because the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value and this deal is the highest-value outcome available
During the Sprint, quality does not decrease, and work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of an Increment and cannot even be presented at the Sprint Review
This is acceptable if the Scrum Master records it as technical debt so it stays visible
This is acceptable because the Definition of Done belongs to the Developers, who may change it whenever they judge it right
questions.explain: Two rules collide with this proposal and both hold: 'Quality does not decrease' during the Sprint, and work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of an Increment. Option A is the most dangerous distractor on this exam, because it quotes your own accountability back at you correctly and then draws a conclusion that undermines the artifact your accountability depends on. Value is not maximized by shipping something you cannot honestly call Done to a buyer who has accessibility requirements in their procurement rules. Option C is the version teams actually run, and naming the damage does not authorize it. Option D misstates the ownership: the Definition of Done is a Scrum Team commitment, and if the organization has a standard, it is a floor nobody may drop below.

questions.stem: Two Scrum Teams work together on the same product. Which THREE of the following does the Scrum Guide require? Select three.
options: They share the same Product Goal
They share the same Product Backlog
They share the same Product Owner
They each maintain a Definition of Done tuned to their own part of the product
They share the same Sprint Backlog so that the plan stays coherent
questions.explain: 'If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.' Option D is contradicted directly: 'If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.' That one is worth remembering because separate quality bars are exactly how a shared product becomes inconsistent. Option E is the opposite error. The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers of one team, so sharing it would break the very self-management that makes each team work.

questions.stem: A pilot must be priced below a specific figure, because above that figure the purchase triggers a formal advertised procurement and a board approval that would add many months. This is a procedural threshold, not a commercial one. How should a Product Owner treat it?
options: As a sales concern outside the product, since Scrum artifacts describe product work only

As a real constraint on what is valuable to build and when, which therefore informs Product Backlog ordering and the Product Goal, since the Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities including stakeholder collaboration
As the Sprint Goal for the next Sprint, so the whole team is aligned to the constraint
As an addition to the Definition of Done, so that every Increment is checked against it
questions.explain: 'The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities from stakeholder collaboration, verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research and development, and anything else that might be required.' A rule that decides whether a customer can buy at all is about as product-related as constraints get, and it changes what a first release must contain. Option A is the tempting one because it sounds like a clean separation of concerns, and it is exactly the separation that produces products nobody can procure. Options C and D both misfile a strategic constraint into a Scrum container built for something else: a Sprint Goal is a single objective for one Sprint, and the Definition of Done is a quality standard for the Increment.

questions.stem: True or false: during a Sprint, scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.
questions.explain: True, and it is one of the four things the Guide lists as holding during a Sprint. This is the sentence that dismantles the most common misunderstanding in Scrum, that a Sprint is a small fixed-scope contract. It is not. What is protected is the Sprint Goal: 'No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal.' The item list is expected to move as the Developers learn what the work really involves, and that renegotiation happens with the Product Owner, inside the Sprint. Notice how this pairs with the Sprint Goal being a commitment that 'provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it'.

questions.stem: The Scrum Guide describes Scrum Teams as self-managing. What does that mean?
options: The team chooses its own Product Goal without reference to stakeholders
The team internally decides who does what, when, and how
The team reports to no manager anywhere in the organization
The team may change its Sprint Goal whenever it decides that circumstances warrant it
questions.explain: 'They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.' Option C is the most tempting because self-managing sounds like organizational independence, and a lot of writing about agility encourages that reading. The Guide's own framing is the opposite: Scrum Teams are 'structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work', which means the organization is very much still there. Option A overreaches into the Product Owner's accountability for the Product Goal. Option D would break the Sprint Goal as a commitment. It is also worth knowing that the 2020 change from self-organizing to self-managing widened the scope to who, how, and what the team works on within its Sprint.

questions.stem: A demo welcome screen offers five entry points and deliberately leaves out the accounts payable clerk, whose daily work the product changes most, on the recorded grounds that she does not sign the contract. Which assessment is most defensible in Scrum terms?
options: It is correct, because the Product Owner maximizes value and the buyer determines whether there is any revenue at all
It is incorrect, because a Product Owner must always order by user value rather than by buyer value

Either ordering can be defensible, and the Product Owner is accountable for making the reasoning transparent so the trade-off can be inspected and adapted, rather than presenting a buyer-driven choice as a user-driven one
The Developers should decide, since they know which persona is cheapest to build for
questions.explain: Scrum does not contain an ordering algorithm. It says the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value and for ordering, and that the Product Owner's decisions must be visible: 'These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog.' So both A and B are attempts to answer a question the framework leaves to your judgment, and B is the more seductive of the two because user-centred thinking feels virtuous. The failure mode Scrum does name is the hidden one: a buyer-driven decision dressed up as a user-driven decision cannot be inspected honestly, and 'artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.' Writing the reason down, as this team did, is the part that was right.

questions.stem: A founder acting as Product Owner also runs sales, and has missed most of the last several Sprint Planning events, sending written notes about priorities instead. What is the most accurate Scrum assessment?
options: This is fine, because the Product Owner may delegate and remains accountable

Sprint Planning's plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team, and the Product Owner ensures attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal; written notes do not satisfy that collaboration
The Scrum Master should run Sprint Planning in the Product Owner's place and define the Sprint Goal from the notes
The Developers should select items themselves and inform the Product Owner of the Sprint Goal afterwards
questions.explain: The plan 'is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team', and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal, which must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning. A Product Owner who is not there cannot answer the trade-off questions that Topic Two turns on, so the Developers either guess or take the notes as orders. Option A is the trap, and it is the best-constructed one in this exam, because both halves of it are true statements from the Guide. Delegation covers the work of Product Backlog management, such as writing and refining items. It does not let you delegate your presence in an event whose output depends on your judgment in the room. Options C and D describe what teams actually do when the Product Owner is absent, and both quietly relocate a product decision to people who do not hold it.
